content: Yellow fever (YF) is a severe viral hemorrhagic disease that occurs primarily in tropical regions of Africa and Latin America. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), there are approximately 200,000 cases of YF annually, resulting in 30,000 deaths worldwide. While there is no specific antiviral treatment for YF, supportive care is provided to manage symptoms. However, a live attenuated virus vaccine has been shown to be effective in preventing YF infection. WHO recommends that all individuals over the age of 9 months who live in or travel to areas where YF is endemic should receive the vaccine. In contrast, the United States Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) advises against administering the YF vaccine to individuals with HIV infection due to concerns about safety and efficacy. This presents a significant challenge, as large populations of people living with HIV reside in regions where YF is endemic. Therefore, the potential role of the YF vaccine in preventing YF among immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV, warrants further investigation. The objective of this study was to evaluate the risks and benefits of YF vaccination in individuals with HIV infection. To achieve this, standard Cochrane methods were employed to search electronic databases and conference proceedings using relevant search terms, without restrictions on language. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials and cohort studies involving HIV-infected individuals who received the YF vaccine (either 17DD or 17D-204 strains). Two authors independently screened the abstracts of 199 references identified through the search process. Of these, 19 studies were examined in detail for eligibility, and three cohort studies were ultimately included in the review. These studies collectively analyzed data from 484 HIV-infected patients who received the YF vaccine. The findings revealed that HIV-infected patients developed significantly lower concentrations of neutralizing antibodies within the first year after vaccination compared to individuals without HIV. However, the rate of antibody decline over time was similar between the two groups. Importantly, none of the HIV-infected patients included in the studies experienced serious adverse events as a result of YF vaccination. The authors concluded that the YF vaccine is capable of inducing protective levels of neutralizing antibodies in individuals with HIV infection. However, the immunogenicity of the vaccine is slightly reduced in HIV-infected patients compared to those without HIV. No serious adverse events related to the vaccine were observed in the HIV-infected participants. The study also highlighted that higher CD4 cell counts and lower levels of HIV RNA at the time of vaccination were associated with better immune responses and the development of protective antibody levels. Despite these findings, the quality of the evidence was rated as low to very low due to the limited number of studies and participants. Nevertheless, the results suggest that the YF vaccine may be safely administered to HIV-infected individuals, provided that HIV replication is well-controlled. To maximize the vaccine's effectiveness, it is recommended that HIV-infected patients receive the YF vaccine only after achieving suppression of HIV replication.
